t.2.51.1: When Rāma had reached the southern bank, Guha, deeply stricken with sorrow, talked for a long while with Sumantra and then went to his own home.
t.2.51.2: Then Sumantra, having been given leave, yoked the finest horses and, deeply downcast, set out for the city of Ayodhyā itself.
t.2.51.3: Gazing upon fragrant forests, rivers and lakes, he swiftly passed by villages and towns.
t.2.51.4: Then, at evening time on the third day, the charioteer reached Ayodhyā and saw that it was joyless.
t.2.51.5: Seeing the city silent, as if deserted, Sumantra, deeply dejected and struck by the force of grief, began to reflect.
t.2.51.6: "I hope the city, with its elephants and horses, its people and its king, has not been consumed by the fire of grief, by the sorrow of anguish over Rāma!" Absorbed in such thoughts, the charioteer hastily entered.
t.2.51.7: Then, as Sumantra drew near, men by the hundreds and by the thousands rushed toward the charioteer, asking, "Where is Rāma?"
t.2.51.8: He told them: "Having taken leave of Rāghava at the Gaṅgā, I have returned, dismissed by that righteous, great-souled one."
t.2.51.9: Learning that they had crossed over, the people, their faces streaming with tears, sighed, "Alas, shame!" and cried out, "Ah, Rāma!"
t.2.51.10: And he heard the words of those who stood about in groups upon groups: "Truly we are ruined, we who no longer see Rāghava here!"
t.2.51.11: Never again shall we see the righteous Rāma in our midst at almsgivings, sacrifices and weddings, or at great assemblies.
t.2.51.12: "What is fitting for these people, what is dear to them, what will bring them happiness?" With such thoughts Rāma protected the city like a father.
t.2.51.13: And all along the market streets he heard the lamentation of the women standing at the windows, burning with grief for Rāma.
t.2.51.14: Sumantra, his face covered, went along the middle of the royal road straight to that very palace where King Daśaratha was.
t.2.51.15: Swiftly descending from the chariot and entering the royal palace, he passed through the seven courtyards, crowded with a great multitude of people.
t.2.51.16: Then, from the palaces on every side, he heard the faint murmuring of Daśaratha's wives, who were burning with grief for Rāma.
t.2.51.17: Having set out together with Rāma and come back here without Rāma, what indeed will the charioteer say in reply to the grieving Kausalyā?
t.2.51.18: And as I think, life will be hard to bear; surely it is not easy for Kausalyā to go on living in such a state, now that her son has torn himself away and departed.
t.2.51.19: Hearing those words of the king's women, which had the very form of truth, he swiftly entered the palace, which seemed as though ablaze with grief.
t.2.51.20: Entering the eighth courtyard, he saw the king in the white palace, wretched and afflicted, worn down by grief for his son.
t.2.51.21: Approaching the lord of men as he sat there and saluting him, Sumantra reported Rāma's words exactly as they had been spoken.
t.2.51.22: Hearing that, the king, his mind bewildered, remained silent; overwhelmed by grief for Rāma, he fainted and fell to the ground.
t.2.51.23: Then, when the lord of the earth had fainted and the king had fallen to the ground, the women's quarters, stricken with grief, raised their arms and cried aloud.
t.2.51.24: Then Kausalyā, together with Sumitrā, raised up her fallen husband and spoke these words.
t.2.51.25: O illustrious one, why do you not speak to this messenger of him who has done so hard a thing, the one who has come back from his dwelling in the forest?
t.2.51.26: Having committed this wrong today, you are ashamed, O Rāghava. Rise, may merit be yours; in grief there can be no help.
t.2.51.28: Having spoken thus to the great king, Kausalyā, overwhelmed by grief, her words choked with tears, quickly fell to the ground.
t.2.51.27: O lord, Kaikeyī, for fear of whom you do not question the charioteer about Rāma, is not here; let him be spoken to freely.
t.2.51.29: Seeing Kausalyā lamenting thus, fallen upon the ground, and looking upon their husband, all those women wept aloud.
t.2.51.30: Then, perceiving that lament which had risen from the inner apartments, the men, old and young, and all the women wept on every side, and the city was once again thrown into turmoil.
